articles.headline: Stage Notes
articles.text:
Each week shows an increase of business transacted by the Medora Stage and Forwarding company, and when the improvements now being made are completed, the new line can carry passengers, freight and express matters in less time and better shape than any other route entering the Hills. Manager Packard reports everything progressing finely and is confident that when the public learns the manner in which this route handles everything entrusted to its care, they will not be slow in taking the many advantages it affords.

Already large shipments of freight have been made, and the freighters will leave for the Hills to-day heavily loaded. The last trip was the fastest ever made from the line of Northern Pacific railroad, and those who know say they can beat the time a day or so.

A mail route is to be established between Spearfish and Carbonate Camp, a distance of seven miles.

Bad weather has interrupted the business of some of the stage lines, but the Medora line seems to be especially favored in this respect. Very little snow falls in this region, and no trouble is anticipated from snow storms.

Taking everything into consideration, the Medora Stage and Forwarding Company is a success in every particular, and there are no good reasons why it should continue to be so.
articles.summary: Stage Notes: business of the Medora Stage and Forwarding Company is growing, freighters leave for the Black Hills heavily loaded, and a Spearfish-Carbonate Camp mail route is planned.

articles.text: A report that the Montana "stranglers" were on their way to Medora caused considerable talk, and all kinds of rumors were afloat. Last week they captured an innocent cow boy and held him in custody for two days. He says he could not convince them that he was honest, nor would they listen to anything he said, but knew everything. It seems strange that men from other territories should come to Dakota to hunt for cattle thieves, when it would keep an army of men very busy for a long time to eliminate that element from their own borders. Medora is able to take care of her own stock, and can dispense with the aid of the "stranglers," as they style themselves. A horse thief stands no show, nor does he deserve any, but to take men who are looking for estrayed stock and string them up a couple of times in order to get information, is going a little too far, and there is likely to be trouble should they attempt anything like that around here. If a man is caught stealing stock, give him the benefit of the noose; but unless a clear case is against him he should have a chance to prove his innocence. It is hoped that they exercise a little more precaution in the future.
articles.summary: Editorial on rumors that Montana vigilante "stranglers" were headed to Medora after they held an innocent cowboy for two days.

articles.text: The cow boy's cure for snoring is unique and effectual if not soothing. On the Utah & Northern railroad last Sunday a 200-pound man lay snoring on two facing seats. His roar had been heard to the discomfort of a carfull all afternoon. At about 4 p. m a cow boy got on at one of the canyon stations. He heard the foghorn with evident impatience for a half hour or so, when he stepped up to the sleeper and said: "Say, stranger, stop that 'ar snort or you'll get fired." The cow boy was not large, but he was full of guns and there was business in his eye. The big man said nothing but lay still, and his sleep, if he slept, was as quiet as the slumber of infancy.—[Dallas, Ore., Letter.
articles.summary: Reprinted anecdote of a cowboy silencing a snoring passenger on the Utah & Northern railroad.

articles.text: A large train of the smallest bulls that was ever seen in the world came in yesterday with freight from Belfield. The diminutiveness of many of them attracted the attention of the crowd. Charley Shanklin inquired of one of the teamsters where the mothers of those calves were, supposing they had been brought along to furnish milk for them. He was answered with a — stare.—[Black Hill Pioneer.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Black Hills Pioneer about a bull train arriving with freight from Belfield.

articles.text: A colony of fifty settlers from Connecticut, under the patronage of P. T. Barnum, have bought a tract of land in Barnes county, Dakota, and will settle there in the spring. Nothing seems to effect permanently the Dakota boom. The growth of the great territory, soon to be a state, is something [phenomenal?].—[St. Paul day.
articles.summary: Reprint: a Connecticut colony backed by P. T. Barnum has bought land in Barnes county, Dakota.

articles.text: From present appearances it will not be long before we have telegraphic communication with Medora. A contract has been let to a Spearfish party to furnish the poles on the ground for the entire distance, and they are now being cut and peeled.—]Black Hills Pioneer.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Black Hills Pioneer: poles are being cut for a telegraph line to Medora.

articles.text: The weather in this vicinity continues very fine. We have had a couple of cloudy days, but no cold has been experienced, and cattle men are taking advantage of it and are getting things in good shape for their stock.
articles.summary: Fine fall weather continues around Medora and cattlemen are preparing for winter.

articles.text: Considerable interest is manifested here as to the result of next Tuesday's election. The republicans are very confident, and claim that the victory in Ohio virtually settles all chances of the democrats.
articles.summary: Local interest in the coming presidential election; republicans are confident.

articles.text: W. F. Storey, proprietor of the Chicago Times, died on Tuesday last. He had been in poor health for some time.
articles.summary: Death of W. F. Storey of the Chicago Times.

articles.text: The silver bullion shipments from Carbonate Camp are expected to amount to 360,000 pounds per month.
articles.summary: Expected silver bullion shipments from Carbonate Camp.

articles.text: President Arthur, it is said, is an aspirant for senator from a New York district.
articles.summary: Report that President Arthur seeks a Senate seat.

articles.headline: Stock Notes.
articles.text:
$250 REWARD.

The above reward will be paid for information leading to the arrest of any person or persons setting fire to the grass in the cattle sections of Western Dakota.

N. P. Ref. Car Co.
Continental Cattle Co.
Hughes & Simpson.
Dorr Clark.
Clark & Plum.
Dickey Bros.
E. G. Paddock.
articles.summary: Seven cattle outfits offer $250 for the arrest of anyone setting prairie fires in western Dakota.

articles.headline: $50 Reward.
articles.text:
$50 Reward.

The above reward will be paid for the return of the following stock or a proportionate reward will be paid for the return of any of them. The stock consists of the following horses:

One bay mare, one brown mare and one roan mare, all young and branded double or reverse P on left shoulder as advertised in our brand columns. Also one light sorrel pony, white legs and face and branded NC on left shoulder and triangle JP on right shoulder also as advertised in our brand columns.

Gregor Lang,
Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: Gregor Lang offers $50 for the return of three mares and a sorrel pony.

articles.headline: Lost—$10 Reward.
articles.text:
Lost from the Little Missouri round-up, one bay horse 5 years old, branded J on left shoulder and S on right flank; partly broken and very wild when he left; had picket rope around neck. Any one returning or giving information of him will receive the above reward.

W. N. Thompson & Co.,
Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: W. N. Thompson & Co. offer $10 for a bay horse lost from the Little Missouri round-up.

articles.headline: Estrayed.
articles.text: A large sorrel horse, branded H G on left hip and cross Y (see M. S. & F. Co.'s brand in brand column) on left shoulder. The above horse strayed from Rocky Ridge station on the Medora stage line October 5. A reward of $10 will be paid for information leading to his recovery.
articles.summary: A Medora stage line horse strayed from Rocky Ridge station on October 5; $10 reward.

articles.text: Jay-Eye-See's new sulky weighs forty-one pounds, and is painted purple, to match Bither's suit.
articles.summary: Trotting-horse note about Jay-Eye-See's new sulky.

articles.text: In Western Montana, a contagious disease called catarrhal is causing considerable trouble among horses.
articles.summary: Catarrhal disease among horses in western Montana.

articles.text: The British authorites, report the almost total eradication of foot and mouth disease in that country.
articles.summary: British report foot and mouth disease nearly eradicated.

articles.text: Parties desiring rules and regulations governing the coming Fat Stock show at Chicago should address the secretary of the state board of agriculture, Springfield, Ill.
articles.summary: Notice about the Chicago Fat Stock show.

articles.text: The corn crop for the present year is placed by the national department of agriculture at the enormous figures of 1,800,000,000 bushels. This should fatten a great many steers.
articles.summary: Record national corn crop estimate.

articles.text: The cattle shipments over the Northern Pacific from July 20th to October 25th amounts to 2,896 cars. The number of cattle carried is 74,920. It is expected that 3,500 cars will be shipped by November 15.
articles.summary: Northern Pacific cattle shipments for the season: 2,896 cars and 74,920 head through October 25.

articles.text: The country up around Spearfish and near Jennie's stockade is fast settling up. A party of land prospectors from this place have just returned, and are very much pleased with the country.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprint on settlement near Spearfish and Jennie's stockade.

articles.text: W. H. Robinson of cleveland Ohio, obtained a verdict of $5,000 and costs against Amos Rank, Joel Sharp, et. al., for infringing on his patent of an appliance for feeding and watering cattle in railroads cars. Others suits will follow.
articles.summary: Patent verdict over a stock-car feeding device.

articles.text: While Colorado will require, ere another harvest, a million bushels of oats for feed, it has not produced to exceed 25,000 bushels. The farmer who has raised wheat that is so far in excess of the demand should give this a thought.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Colorado oats shortage.

articles.text: There has been less of scab this year among the flocks of Colorado than in any prior year. The flock owners are paying better attention than heretofore, knowing that it will not do to be so careless of an animal that requires the best of attention to prosper.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Less sheep scab in Colorado.

articles.text: The Chicago stock yards were constructed about twenty years ago, and are the largest in the world. They are capable of accommodating 20,000 cattle, 150,000 hogs, 10,000 sheep, and 1,500 horses. Seventeen different railroads center in the yards. It is estimated that the number of car loads received and shipped last year would make about 9,000 trains of thirty-one cars each. If placed in one train they would reach from New York to St. Louis and back, a distance of about 2,146 miles.
articles.summary: Facts about the Chicago stock yards.

articles.text: Experiments have been made in England as to the comparative value of good hay and stock, with the result that it is estimated that 100 pounds of hay are equal to 275 pounds of green Indian corn, 400 pounds of green clover, 442 pounds of rye straw, 360 pounds of wheat straw, 160 pounds of oat straw, 180 pounds of barley straw, 153 pounds of pea straw, 200 pounds of buckwheat straw, 400 pounds of dried corn stalks, 175 pounds of raw potatoes, 504 pounds of turnips, 300 pounds of carrots, 54 pounds of rye, 46 pounds of wheat, 59 pounds of oats, 45 pounds of mixed peas and beans, 64 pounds of buckwheat, 57 pounds of Indian corn, 68 pounds of acorns, 105 pounds of wheat bran, 167 pounds of wheat, pea, and oat chaff, 179 pounds of mixed rye and barley, 59 pounds of linseed, and 330 pounds of mangel-wurzel.—[Scientific American.
articles.summary: Feed-value equivalents of hay from English experiments.

articles.text: About thirty-five per cent. of cattle of Illinois are classed as high grade by the department of agriculture. By high grade is meant those having more than half blood of some of the recognized pure breeds. The increase of value from this source alone is $20,000,000.
articles.summary: High-grade cattle in Illinois.

articles.text: Gov. Cleveland is about to start on an exhibition tour to advertise the advantages of New York as a stock-raising state. He expects to take the first prize at Newark. A special stock car is provided. He is the first Jersey product ever nomitated for the presidential office.
articles.summary: Political joke casting Gov. Cleveland as livestock.

articles.text: Any cow can be milked dry in a few weeks by irregular milking, sometimes at intervals of twenty-four hours and sometimes of six. Separation from her usual company, a change to new location, a strange milker and scolding voice, are sources of irritation that more or less impair the milking qualities of a cow.
articles.summary: Dairy advice on milking.

articles.text: A cane made entirely of the horns of cattle has been presented to Major Rainwater, of St. Louis, chairman of the executive committe of the national convention of cattle men that meets in St. Louis next month. He is also to be given a chair, the frame of which will be composed of the horns of Texas cattle, and will occupy it on the platform.
articles.summary: Horn cane and chair for Major Rainwater of the national cattlemen's convention in St. Louis.

articles.text: A citizen of Tarrant county, Colorado, whose wife was sick, wishing to go for his daughter, who was sixty miles distant on a visit, in the absence of a horse, rode a two-year-old bull, making the round trip—120 miles—in forty-eight hours. He said the bovine was rather too poor to ride without a saddle, and as he expressed it, "putty bad gittin on agin after the wind strikes me awhile."
articles.summary: Anecdote of a man riding a bull 120 miles.

articles.text: The calf crop is surprising the cattlemen in northern New Mexico, and is likely to make up for the discouraging shortage last spring. From as reliable an informant as Col. Dwyer, of Colfax we learn that the calf branding of the last round-up in this neighborhood was much larger than was ever known in the fall season here before, and that the shortage of the first round-up will be more than made up.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Large fall calf crop in northern New Mexico.

articles.text: It is the opinion of many of the larger cattle holders upon the plains that the death losses in winters will not exceed two per cent., if a term of ten years be taken into account. The winters of 1880 and '81 were severe and the loss was not less than four per cent. of all the cattle upon the open plains, but in '82 it did not exceed one and a half. In '83 it went to three. For several winters prior to 1880 it did not exceed one and a half per cent.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Estimated winter death losses of range cattle on the plains.

articles.text: The Garden City Irrigator says a man south of us was approached lately by a "granger" who wished to buy a cow. It so happened that the c. m. had an old cow that had seen her best days, and being in sight of the ranch they rode out to look at her. She was pretty well covered with brands of various descriptions, and most awful poor. The granger walked around her a time or two and then remarked, "She isn't much of a cow." "No," said the c. m. "but [she's?] got lots of good reading on her."
articles.summary: Joke about a heavily branded cow.

articles.text: The wintering of sheep depends much on the condition of the flock at the beginning of winter, remarks the Michigan Farmer. Sheep that are low in flesh in the fall hardly ever improve, but keep going down hill all along, until before the spring time draws around their pelts are hanging in the shade. See, then, that your flocks are in good condition, and if there are any thin ones among them, separate them from the rest and give them a little grain each day until they have gained their wonted vigor.
articles.summary: Advice on wintering sheep.

articles.text: If there is one class of men in this world more noted than another for honesty, we believe it is the editors. The habit of appropriating cattle belonging to another when favorable opportunity offers is entirely too popular, but this is a crime of which an editor would not be guilty, at least this appears to be the case with Brother Hays, of the Avalanche published a Silver City, Idaho. He thus cries out: "Somebody's calf, with somebody's brand on it is sucking our cow. Take the calf away, for it is not ours."—[N. W. L. Journal.
articles.summary: Joke about an Idaho editor and a stray calf.

articles.text: The American race horse Foxhall that created such a sensation in Europe three years ago by winning the grand prize of Paris, the Cambrigeshire and the Czarewhitch, has been sold by Mr. J. R. Keene to Lord Rosebery, the price being $20,000. The purchaser recently returned from a trip around the world, and in the course of his journey witnessed the performances of American and Australian horses, and therefore the selection, on returning home, of an American-bred one to place at the head of his stud farm is a decided compliment to this country.
articles.summary: Sale of the race horse Foxhall to Lord Rosebery.

articles.text: To a hard-working horse, repose is almost as much as good food; but tired though he may be, he is often very shy to lie down, even when a clean bed has been provided for him. Unless a horse lies down regularly, his rest is never complete, and his joints and sinews stiffen; and while it is true that some horses that sleep in a standing position continue to work for many years, it is equally true that they would wear much longer, and perform their work much better, if they rested naturally. Young, nervous horses not infrequently refuse to lie down when first made to occupy a stall, and, when introduced into a town stable, the habit may become confirmed, unless inducements are offered to overcome the disinclination.—[Reynolds on Draught Horses.
articles.summary: Advice on getting horses to lie down and rest.

Ready-print page: paper's nameplate over syndicated editorials (presidential canvass, Belva Lockwood, Atlantic steamers, Galway, prime meridian conference), "The Pith of the News" wire digest, "Republican Campaign News" (prohibition and Blaine campaign matter), fiction and miscellany ("Dreams and Dreamers," "Personal Gossip").

Ready-print page: syndicated "Territorial News Notes" from elsewhere in Dakota, election candidate lists, a medical curiosity piece, "Senator Anthony's Library," a railroad anecdote, and patent-medicine and mail-order ads (Cuticura, Perry Davis' Pain-Killer, Hostetter's Bitters, Tutt's Pills, St. Jacobs Oil, Kidney-Wort, Pioneer Press, Chicago Globe).

articles.summary: Editorial-page heading and time tables for the Medora and Black Hills stage line and the Northern Pacific at Medora.

articles.text: Will Kidd left on Wednesday for the east.
articles.summary: Will Kidd leaves for the east.

articles.text: A roller rink will be opened in Roberts' hall.
articles.summary: A roller rink will open in Roberts' hall.

articles.text: Dr. Jorgens will arrive the first of next week.
articles.summary: Dr. Jorgens expected early next week.

articles.text: Bob Roberts had the south side of his building raised.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts raises part of his building.

articles.text: Tilden R. Selmes and wife, of Mandan, were in town on Monday.
articles.summary: Tilden R. Selmes and wife of Mandan visit Medora.

articles.text: The Marquis received an order for 500 cattle from a Chicago firm.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès receives an order for 500 cattle from Chicago.

articles.text: The erection of the N. P. R. C. Co.'s slaughter house will be commenced shortly.
articles.summary: The N. P. R. C. Co. slaughter house will soon be built.

articles.text: A large number of geese passed over Medora during the past week on their way south.
articles.summary: Geese migrating south over Medora.

articles.text: J. A. Ferris must do a rushing business, judging from the amount of printing he has done.
articles.summary: J. A. Ferris's business is brisk, judging by his printing orders.

articles.text: Dan McKenzie, the blacksmith, has been quite busy of late. He says work is picking up again.
articles.summary: Blacksmith Dan McKenzie reports more work.

articles.text: The damage caused by fire to Hotel de Mores has been repaired, and everything is running smoothly.
articles.summary: Fire damage at the Hotel de Mores has been repaired.

articles.text: Mr. Lloyd Roberts brought two cars of cattle for the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car company on Wednesday.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts brings two cars of cattle for the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.

articles.text: Vic Smith brought in another lot of antelope, coyotes and mountain deer. Vic never comes home empty-handed.
articles.summary: Hunter Vic Smith brings in more game.

articles.text: A herd of buffalo was seen about twenty-five miles southwest of here on Tuesday. Several of our hunters went out after them.
articles.summary: Buffalo herd sighted 25 miles southwest of Medora.

articles.text: Sam Townsend returned from the Hills Sunday making the round trip in 21 days. A broken wheel caused a delay of two days.
articles.summary: Sam Townsend returns from the Black Hills after a 21-day round trip.

articles.text: Baron Von Steiger brought in some very fine potatoes for the company's store. Billings county is not slow in raising potatoes.
articles.summary: Baron Von Steiger brings potatoes to the company store.

articles.text: The report that a cow boy well known around here was drawn up three times by the Montana "stranglers" seems to be without foundation.
articles.summary: Report that a local cowboy was hanged up three times by Montana stranglers is called unfounded.

articles.text: Lee Eisenberg, representing the house of Dan Eisenberg, Bismarck, transacted considerable business in Medora on Saturday. Lee is a rustler.
articles.summary: Bismarck salesman Lee Eisenberg does business in Medora.

articles.text: Mr. E. Elmer's family arrived from Jamestown on Wednesday. Mr. Elmer will open up a place of business on the other side of the river.
articles.summary: E. Elmer's family arrives from Jamestown; he will open a business across the river.

articles.text: Next Sunday morning at 9:30 the new Catholic church will be blessed, and mass celebrated. The Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan will officiate.
articles.summary: The new Catholic church in Medora will be blessed next Sunday.

articles.text: Work on the foundation of the new cooler has been temporarily delayed by the non-arrival of cement. It was to have been finished this week.
articles.summary: Cooler foundation work delayed for lack of cement.

articles.text: Hotel de Mores is having a good run of business. Mr. Fitzgerald tries to please everybody, and his efforts are appreciated by all who stop with him.
articles.summary: Hotel de Mores doing good business under Mr. Fitzgerald.

articles.text: Mr. T. Smith is out looking for an estrayed horse. The animal belongs to the stage line and is a valuable one. See notice of reward in another column.
articles.summary: T. Smith searches for a strayed stage-line horse.

articles.text: The drug store is being put in first class shape. A large supply of new goods have been received. The public is invited to call and examine them.
articles.summary: The drug store receives new goods.

articles.text: The Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car company received a large order for beef from Chicago. It will only be a short while before the company will work up a large business there.
articles.summary: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. receives a large beef order from Chicago.

articles.text: The time of the passenger trains will probably be changed on the 1st of November. The east bound train will arrive in the evening and the west bound train in the early morning.
articles.summary: Passenger train schedule expected to change November 1.

articles.text: The town well is almost completed, and the quality of the water is very good. It is just the thing for lemonade, to say nothing about washing windows, etc. Some say it is even good to drink, but we never saw them tackle water, and do not consider them the best of authority.
articles.summary: The Medora town well is nearly complete.

articles.text: Mr. Malloy, of the Western House, Little Missouri, has been very busy getting his hotel in first class shape for the winter. His cellars are filled with all kinds of eatables, and he is prepared to feed an army of hungry people. Mr. Malloy knows how to please his guests, and he never tires of doing so.
articles.summary: Peter Malloy readies the Western House for winter.

articles.text: Quite a number of our young people attended the dance given in honor of Mr. N. A. Thayer, at the Pyramid Park hotel, Little Missouri, Tuesday night. All kinds of refreshments were served, and the affair was one which will not be soon forgotten. Excellent music was furnished by Gill Kennedy and Joe Dulgyee.
articles.summary: Dance for N. A. Thayer at the Pyramid Park hotel.

articles.text: A man named Michael Strang, about 40 years of age, was brought to town on Sunday, charged with setting fire to the grass on the range about four miles southeast of here. He was taken to Mandan, where he was bound over to await the action of the district court. It is about time that someone should be punished for this offense.
articles.summary: Michael Strang charged with setting a range fire, bound over at Mandan.

articles.text: Rassie Deffenbach, of the Medora stage line, went to Belfield Wednesday.
articles.summary: Rassie Deffenbach of the stage line goes to Belfield.

articles.text: The switches in this vicinity are being repaired. N. A. Thayer it superintending the work.
articles.summary: Railroad switches near Medora being repaired under N. A. Thayer.

articles.text: As to-day's emigrant train was pulling out, the track spread and two cars were derailed. The damage was slight, and little delay was accasioned.
articles.summary: Two cars of the emigrant train derailed at Medora.

articles.text: Mr. J. A. Field was here on Saturday collecting petrifactions for the New Orleans exposition. Billings county will show up well in that line, also in game and agricultural products.
articles.summary: J. A. Field collects petrifactions for the New Orleans exposition.

articles.text: When the roller rink opens there will be some great feats performed. There will be a contest between such artists as John Warn, Pat O'Hare and other well known local celebrities.
articles.summary: Roller rink contest planned.

articles.text: General Manager Packard, of the Medora Stage and Forwarding Company, is still in the Hills in the interest of the stage company. He reports everything in good shape. He is [expected?] back [the?] latter part of this week.
articles.summary: A. T. Packard is still in the Black Hills on stage company business.

articles.text: Last Tuesday night one of our young men got too much corn juice aboard and, while in this condition, attempted to gain an entrance into the house opposite his, thinking it was his own, when two shots were fired at him, the bullets whizzing by his head. He says it was a close shave, and that he will be more careful in the future.
articles.summary: Drunk young man shot at while entering the wrong house.
